title: A Proof that Reed-Muller Codes Achieve Shannon Capacity on Symmetric Channels
abstract: In 1948, Shannon used a probabilistic argument to show that there exist codes achieving a maximal rate defined by the channel capacity. In 1954, Muller and Reed introduced a simple deterministic code construction, conjectured shortly after to achieve channel capacity. Major progress was made towards establishing this conjecture over the last decades, with various branches of discrete mathematics involved such as combinatorial bounds, sharp thresholds, hypercontractivity, additive combinatorics and polarization theory. In particular, the special case of the erasure channel was settled by Kudekar at al., relying on Bourgain-Kalai’s sharp threshold theorem for symmetric monotone properties. The main case of error channels remained however unsettled, due in particular to the property being non-monotone, despite the vanishing local error result from Reeves-Pfister. This paper closes the general conjecture's proof. The main ingredient is a new recursive boosting framework for coding, where codewords are decoded by aggregating restrictions on a `subspace-sunflower' structure, analogous to the structure from Erd\H{o}s-Rado 1960. The dependencies on the sunflower petals are handled with an $L_p$ Boolean Fourier analysis to achieve fast local error decay, and a list-decoding argument with a weight enumerator bound from Sberlo-Shpilka is used to control the global error from the local one. For the local error, the proof circumvents the use of Bourgain-Kalai's result by establishing first a `weak threshold' result for the local error using solely symmetries. This gives in particular a shortened and tightened argument for the vanishing local error result, and with prior works, it implies the strong wire-tap secrecy of RM codes on pure-state classical-quantum channels.

Abstract—In 1948, Shannon used a probabilistic argument to
show that there exist codes achieving a maximal rate defined by
the channel capacity. In 1954, Muller and Reed introduced a
simple deterministic code construction, conjectured shortly after
to achieve channel capacity. Major progress was made towards
establishing this conjecture over the last decades, with various
branches of discrete mathematics involved such as combinatorial
bounds, sharp thresholds, hypercontractivity, additive combinatorics and polarization theory. In particular, the special case
of the erasure channel was settled by Kudekar at al., relying
on Bourgain-Kalai’s sharp threshold theorem for symmetric
monotone properties. The main case of error channels remained
however unsettled, due in particular to the property being nonmonotone and the lack of techniques to obtain fast local error
decay up to capacity, despite the notable vanishing bound on the
local error from Reeves-Pfister.
This paper closes the conjecture’s proof. The main ingredient is
a new recursive boosting framework for coding, where codewords
are decoded by aggregating restrictions on a ‘subspace-sunflower’
structure, analogous to the structure from Erdős-Rado 1960.
The dependencies between the sunflower petals are handled with
an L2 and L4 Boolean Fourier analysis, and a list-decoding
argument with a weight enumerator bound from Sberlo-Shpilka
is used to control the global error from the local one. For the
local error, while monotonicity does not apply, we show that a
‘weak threshold’ result still holds using solely symmetries. This
gives in particular a shortened and tightened argument for the
vanishing local error result, and with prior works, it also implies
the strong wire-tap secrecy of RM codes on pure-state classicalquantum channels.
Index Terms—Coding, Shannon capacity, Reed-Muller codes,
boosting, sunflowers, Fourier analysis, symmetries, thresholds.

I. I NTRODUCTION
Shannon introduced in 1948 the notion of channel capacity
[Sha48], as the largest rate at which messages can be reliably
transmitted over a noisy channel. In particular, for the canonical binary symmetric channel which flips every coordinate
of a codeword independently with probability ϵ, Shannon’s
capacity is 1 − H(ϵ), where H is the binary entropy function.
To show that the capacity is achievable, Shannon used a
probabilistic argument, i.e., a code drawn uniformly at random.
In the ‘worst-case’ or ‘Hamming’ setting [Ham50], random
codes can also be used to show that rates up to 1 − H(2ϵ)
are achievable1 , as codewords there must produce a packing

reach higher rates due to rare error events being tolerated.
Obtaining explicit code constructions achieving these limits
has since then generated decades of research activity across
electrical engineering, computer science and mathematics.
a) A simple explicit code: The Reed-Muller code was
introduced by Muller in 1954 [Mul54], and is one of the first
and simplest codes. Reed developed shortly after a decoding
algorithm succeeding up to half its minimum distance [Ree54].
The code construction can be described with a greedy procedure. Consider the construction of a subspace of Fn2 (a linear
code) with blocklength given by a power of two, n = 2m .
One can naturally start with the all-0 codeword. If one has
to pick a second codeword, then the all-1 codeword is the
best choice under most relevant criteria. If one has to now
keep these two codewords, the next best choice to maximize
the code distance is a codeword with half-0 and half-1, and to
continue building a basis sequentially, one can add a few more
vectors of weight n/2 to preserve a relative distance of half,
completing the Reed-Muller RM (m, 1) code of order 1 (also
called the (augmented) Hadamard code). This has excellent
distance/rate tradeoff, but it may be now less clear how to
pick the next codeword. One can however simply iterate the
previous construction on the support of the previously picked
codewords, reducing each time the distance by half. This gives
the RM (m, r) code, whose basis is equivalently defined by
the evaluation vectors of monomials of degree at most r on
m Boolean variables:
RM (m, r) = {(f (0m ), . . . , f (1m )) : f ∈ F2 (X1 , . . . , Xm ),
deg(f ) ≤ r}.
As mentioned, the first order RM code RM (m, 1) is the
augmented Hadamard or simplex code code. The simplex code
is the dual of the Hamming code that is ‘perfect’, i.e., it
provides a perfect sphere-packing of the space (it achieves
the sphere-packing bound). This strong property is clearly lost
for general RM codes, but RM codes preserve nonetheless
a decent distance (at root block length for constant rate). In
the worst-case model, where the distance controls the errordecoding capabilities, the RM code does not give a ‘good’
family of codes (i.e., a family of codes with asymptotically

B. Progress and related references
We now overview the main progress on the conjecture in
rough chronological order.
1) [SP92] is one of the first work establishing performance
guarantees for RM codes in the Shannon setting, but
for fixed r and with an offset compared to the capacity
scaling. A first capacity-achieving scaling is obtained
in [HKL05] for the special case of r = 1, 2. Around
that time, a line of work by Dummer also makes major
progress on the RM code recursive decoding [Dum04],
[DS06], [Dum06], albeit without capacity-achieving results. The polar codes breakthrough then takes place in
[Arı09], reviving the conjecture as discussed earlier.
2) The first capacity-achieving result for non-constant r
appears in [ASW15b], [ASW15a], in particular any
r = o(m) for the BSC, which develops the weight
enumerator bound approach for BEC and BSC channels,
leveraging techniques from the key paper [KLP12]. Prior
to [KLP12], a several works in the 70s derived weight
enumerator bounds, from the original work of SloaneBerlekamp for r = 2 [SB70] to regimes with twice
or 2.5 times the minimum distance [KT70], [KTA76].
However, no notable progress had appeared since 1976,
until [KLP12] managed to break through the 2.5 barrier
and provide bounds for distances in a much broader

3) A breakthrough then took place for the binary erasure
channel (BEC), with the celebrated papers [KKM+ 16a],
[KKM+ 17]. The BEC is the simplest non-trivial channel; it does not allow for errors but only erasures. The
BEC benefits in particular from a strong property: the
event of decoding a bit incorrectly given the other noisy
bits is a monotone property on the set of erasure patterns.
This allows [KKM+ 16a] to connect to generic results
from sharp thresholds of monotone properties [FK96],
[BK97] and conclude with an elegant proof that any code
having enough symmetries (namely, doubly transitivity),
is capacity achieving on the BEC. Further, due to the
results of [BK97], under such symmetries, the threshold
must be in fact sharp enough. This implies with a simple
union that the global error is controlled by the local
error. This property and the use of [BK97] are however
lacking for non-BEC channels.
4) In [SS20], an important improvement of [ASW15b]
is obtained, with a similar proof technique but with
tighter and more generic estimates, producing useful
weight enumerator bounds for larger r, in particular the
regime of r inducing constant rates, of interest for the
conjecture. As we shall see, this improvement will turn
out to be key in one step of our proof.
5) While polar codes have revived the activity on the
RM code conjecture, due to their similarity, the prior
progress is based on techniques that have no apparent
relations to polar codes. In [AY19], a connection to polarization theory is developed, showing that by decoding
bits sequentially in the RM code order (by decreasing
weight), the conditional entropy also polarizes. This in
turn implies that the code obtained by retaining the
‘large-entropy’ components, defined as the ‘twin-RM
code’, must be capacity achieving on any BMS channel.
To close the conjecture, it remains to show that this
‘twin-RM’ code is equivalent to the RM code. There appears to be sufficient evidence supporting this –the two
codes are equivalent for the BEC, and numerical simulations as well as partial theoretical results [AHN21]
support it–but that program remains to be closed, with
intriguing connections to additive combinatorics [TV06],
[Lov17], [San12].
6) A new analytical approach was developed in [Sam18],
[Sam20] to obtain bounds for the weight enumerator
of RM codes in new parameter regimes. In particular,
[Sam20] allows to leverage results for erasure channels
to new bounds on the weight enumerator, via hypercontracivity arguments. Improvements on how to exploit the
erasure duality were further developed in [HSS21] which
achieves an important milestone: showing that RM codes
can be decoded at constant rate over the BSC. While
this does not give a capacity result, it settled an open

problem from [ASW15b] as techniques therein did not
seem able to capture this regime.
7) In [YA20], a recursive projection aggregation algorithm
is developed, decoding a codeword by recursively projecting it on subspaces, and aggregating the projection
decodings with a majority vote. While no capacity
results are obtained for this algorithm, which is also limited to low r, some of the high-level ideas of recursively
combining sub-components decoding of the codewords
have a common flavor with the generic boosting procedure developed here. However, we rely here not on
projections but restrictions (which do not suffer from
noise increase) and on the carefully chosen ‘sunflower
subspaces’, to aggregate effectively the restrictions and
to allow for a controlled dependency analysis.
8) Finally, another major result recently showed that the
EXIT function, the probability of decoding a bit incorrectly given the other noisy bits, vanishes below capacity
for RM codes on any BMS channel. The approach of
[RP21] is based on the area theorem and EXIT function
as in [KKM+ 16a], working out more tailored bounds
for BMS channels based on an mmse version of the
EXIT function and the nesting property of RM codes.
While [RP21] appears to come close to establishing the
conjecture, the very slow decay obtained for the EXIT
function prevents the settlement of the conjecture as
discussed next.
We refer to [ASY21], [ASSY23] for further references.
C. From local to global error and the critical part of the proof
As mentioned above, a recent paper [RP21] showed that
at any constant rate below capacity, RM codes achieve a
vanishing ‘bit-error probability’ on all BMSp
channels, with a
bit error scaling at the rate of O(log log(n)/ log(n)). While
this is an important result, such a slow rate does not imply
that RM codes achieves capacity in the classical sense of
recovering the codewords, neither from a union bound nor
from the weight enumerator bounds. In fact, in our boosting
framework, such a slow decay rate would allow us to skip the
first boosting step but is otherwise not much further in the
progress compared to a constant but non-trivial decay, which
we can establish here more directly and more generically as
our base case. The dominant part of the conjecture’s proof
relies on reaching a fast-enough decay to be able to recover
the codewords with list-decoding, which requires a much faster
decay than [RP21].

Some implications of this theorem:

explicit construction of encoding complexity O(n log2 n) that
is universal for all BMS channels of same capacity, can
match the performance of Shannon’s random codes in terms
of achieving capacity with maximum likelihood decoding. We
also refer to Remark 4 for how this can be generalizes to q-ary
symmetric channel.
(ii) Our results also have some implications for quantum
codes. As stated in [Ren18], the binary symmetric channel
is dual to the quantum pure state channel. As such, the fact
that RM codes transmitted through a BSC can be recovered
with high probability whenever the code’s rate is below the
channel’s capacity implies that RM codes achieve strong
secrecy on a wiretap channel using a pure state channel for
the wiretap up to the capacity of the channel. In other words,
consider a channel where an eavesdropper gets access to
the message through a pure state channel. If the message
consists of the XOR of some base message and a random
codeword from an RM code with rate higher than the capacity
of the eavesdropper’s channel then the eavesdropper cannot
distinguish between any two possible base messages with
nontrivial advantage over guessing blindly.
Moreover, as pointed out by [Ren23], our result also implies
that Quantum Reed-Muller codes achieve the so-called coherent information for Pauli channels, and that one can create
a quantum code of Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) type from
two appropriately-chosen RM codes.
Theorem 1 part (i) is proved in Section VII and [AS23];
part (ii) and the adjustment needed to extend the proofs to

IV. C ONCLUSION AND OPEN PROBLEMS
This paper proves the conjecture that RM codes achieve
capacity on all BMS channels, in the classical sense of
recovering the codewords with high probability down to
capacity. It shows that, despite their simple deterministic
channel-independent construction taking Õ(n) time, RM codes
match random codes in universally achieving capacity on BMS
channels.
